[User_Bob]: Hi all, I'm trying to hook up a 12 V LED strip (the cheap kind from Amazon, says 12 V, 0.4 A per meter) to a 12 V wall adapter I have. Do I still need a resistor, and if so, how do I pick the value? I'm confused because the strip already has some little resistors on it.

[User_Alice]: Most 12 V LED strips already have the current-limiting resistors built in for each segment, so if you're running it from a reasonably regulated 12 V supply you usually don't need an extra series resistor. The main thing is to make sure your adapter can supply enough current for the length of strip you're using.

[Other_forum_users]: If your adapter is a bit "hot" (like 12.5–13 V under light load), you can add a small series resistor to be kinder to the LEDs. For 0.4 A, something like 2.2 Ω at a couple watts will drop ~1 V and take the edge off. Measure the actual current if you can.

[User_Bob]: Thanks! The adapter label says 12 V 2 A, but with my multimeter I'm seeing about 12.6 V with no load. If I only use 1 m of strip, would a 2.2 Ω resistor still be okay, and what wattage should I buy so it doesn't get too hot?

Considering safety, a resistor with at least 1W rating is acceptable, but opting for 2W provides a better margin. So, I recommend a 1W or 2W resistor for optimal performance.

**Providing final recommendations**

I should suggest measuring the actual current and checking the temperature; it’s a good idea to mount the resistor on a heatsink or allow it to cool in free air. 2.2 Ω will work for 1 m at ~0.4 A — it will drop about 0.88 V (12.6→~11.7 V) and dissipate ~0.35 W (I^2R).  
A 1 W resistor is technically sufficient, but get a 2 W part for margin so it doesn't run hot.  
Use a power resistor (metal‑oxide or low‑ohm wirewound); metal‑oxide is less inductive and fine for DC.  
Measure the strip current to confirm and check the resistor temperature after a few minutes; if the adapter sags to ~12 V under load you probably don't need the extra resistor.
